name: Hype Cycle
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why Everyone Was So Sure Blockchain Would Change Everything by Now
lesson.summary: Gartner's Hype Cycle explains the predictable rise and fall of excitement around a new technology, and blockchain rode that curve about as textbook as any technology in recent memory.
lesson.body:
The research firm Gartner popularized a simple model for how new technologies are perceived over time, called the Hype Cycle. It has five stages. First comes the Innovation Trigger, when a breakthrough gets its first public attention. Then the Peak of Inflated Expectations, when media coverage and success stories (often based on very little actual deployment) convince everyone the technology will solve nearly every problem. That is followed by the Trough of Disillusionment, when the gap between promises and delivered results becomes impossible to ignore and interest collapses. Eventually, for technologies that survive, comes the Slope of Enlightenment, where realistic, narrower applications start working and quietly proving themselves. Finally there is the Plateau of Productivity, where the technology is just a normal, unremarkable part of how some things get done.

Blockchain followed this arc closely. The Bitcoin white paper in 2008 and Ethereum's programmable smart contracts around 2015 were the innovation trigger. By 2017 and 2018, during the initial coin offering boom, the Peak of Inflated Expectations arrived in force: companies added the word "blockchain" to their names and saw their stock prices jump, consultants promised blockchain would fix supply chains, voting, land titles, medical records, and identity all at once, and it was common to hear that blockchain was as significant an invention as the internet itself. The years that followed brought a slow, less-publicized Trough of Disillusionment, as many of the pilots you will read about in the next several chapters were quietly scaled back or shut down. Notably, Gartner itself eventually stopped publishing a single standalone "Blockchain" Hype Cycle, because by the early 2020s the technology had fragmented into narrower, more specific categories, things like tokenization, decentralized finance, and distributed ledger technology for enterprise, each moving along its own curve rather than one unified blockchain story. That fragmentation is itself a sign of a technology maturing past the point where a single sweeping narrative still makes sense.

This chapter builds directly on cognitive bias and appeal to novelty, because the Hype Cycle is really a description of how those two things play out at industry scale. Appeal to novelty is the reasoning error of assuming something must be better simply because it is newer. During the Peak of Inflated Expectations, that fallacy gets amplified by confirmation bias, where early success stories get repeated and failures get ignored, and by a kind of professional fear of missing out, where executives who did not have a "blockchain strategy" worried they looked behind the times. None of this required anyone to be dishonest. It is simply what happens when a genuinely interesting technology meets ordinary human psychology and a news cycle that rewards bold claims over careful ones.

The practical lesson for a skeptic is not to dismiss new technology, but to ask where on the curve a specific claim sits before deciding how much weight to give it. A press release announcing a blockchain pilot is Peak of Inflated Expectations evidence. A system that has been running in production for several years with public usage data is Slope of Enlightenment or Plateau of Productivity evidence. Learning to tell those apart is exactly the skill the next chapter turns into a formal method, and the case studies after that put it to work on real, named projects.
